t: 3624. Number of Integers With Popcount-Depth Equal to K II — Editorial
o:
## Understanding the problem
Popcount-depth of x: repeatedly replace x by its set-bit count until reaching 1; depth = number of steps (depth(1)=0). Values up to 10¹⁵ have popcount ≤ 50, so depth(x) = 1 + depth(popcount(x)) with depths of 2..50 precomputed — max depth is small (≤ 5 for these bounds). Type-1 queries ask how many nums[j] in [l, r] have depth k (k ≤ 5); type-2 updates assign nums[idx] = val.

With n, q ≤ 10⁵, maintain one Fenwick tree per depth value 0..5: point updates on value change, range sums for queries.
k: depth(x) = 0 if x == 1, else 1 + depth(popcount(x)); precompute depth for 2..63 and answer any x in O(1).
Only 6 distinct depth values occur, so 6 BITs suffice.
Point update + range count is the classic Fenwick pattern; each operation is O(log n).

a.n: Approach 1: Six Fenwick trees over depth values
a.i: Compute each element's depth once. A type-1 query is a prefix-sum difference on tree k. A type-2 update removes the old depth at idx and inserts the new one. Everything is O(log n) per operation.
s: Precompute small-depth table via popcount recurrence.
Build 6 BITs, inserting depth of each initial element.
Type-1 [1,l,r,k]: answer sum(k, r) − sum(k, l−1).
Type-2 [2,idx,val]: decrement old depth at idx, recompute depth(val), increment.
a.t: O((n + q) log n) — each query/update touches one BIT with O(log n) node visits.
a.sp: O(6n) for the six Fenwick trees.

w: Segment trees per depth work equally well; BITs are lighter. Pitfalls: depth(1) = 0 (not 1), using 32-bit popcount on values up to 10¹⁵ (need 64-bit/BigInt), and forgetting to remove the old depth before inserting the new on updates. Follow-up: k up to 60, or range updates of values.
